title: Why Is It So Hard to Get Up in the Morning?
focus: Zero and first conditional, modals of advice
paragraphs: Every morning at six forty, Ravi's alarm rings, and every morning he presses the snooze button three times. He isn't lazy. According to sleep scientists, he is simply a normal teenager whose body is working exactly as nature designed it.

Inside our brain there is a 'body clock' that tells us when to feel awake and when to feel sleepy. During the teenage years, this clock changes. Teenagers' bodies release melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, later at night than the bodies of children or adults. As a result, many teenagers don't feel tired until eleven o'clock or even later.

The problem is that most schools start early. A teenager who goes to bed at midnight and wakes up at six thirty sleeps only six and a half hours, but doctors say that people between thirteen and eighteen need about eight to ten hours. If they don't get enough sleep, they find it harder to concentrate, and they often feel more irritable.
Screens can make things worse. The bright light from a phone tells the brain that it is still daytime, so falling asleep takes longer. And scrolling for ten minutes in bed can easily become an hour.

What can you do? First, go to bed at the same time every night, even at the weekend. Second, leave your phone in another room an hour before sleeping. Third, avoid energy drinks and coffee in the afternoon. Finally, open the curtains as soon as you wake up, because daylight helps to reset your body clock. If you follow these tips for two weeks, you will probably notice a difference. Some schools have even tried starting lessons later, and many of them say that students are calmer and less tired.
glossary: botón de repetición de la alarma

title: Building an Altar for the Day of the Dead
paragraphs: Many people think that the Day of the Dead is a sad holiday, but in my family it is a time to remember with love and even with laughter. Every year, at the end of October, we build an altar in the living room of our house in Oaxaca. This year my teacher asked me to explain the tradition to my class, so I made a presentation about our altar.

An altar, or ofrenda, has several levels. At the top we put photos of the people we want to remember. This year there are pictures of my great-grandfather, who used to play the guitar, and my aunt Rosa, who used to make the best tamales in the neighbourhood. We also place candles because the light helps the spirits find their way home.

Flowers are very important. We use marigolds, called cempasúchil, which have a strong smell and a bright orange colour. Some families make a path of petals from the street to the altar. My brother and I bought three bunches at the market for forty pesos each, and we spent an afternoon pulling off the petals.

Food comes next. According to the tradition, the spirits come back for a short visit and enjoy the favourite dishes of their lives. So we prepare pan de muerto, a sweet bread, a cup of hot chocolate and some fruit for my great-grandfather. Of course, we eat everything afterwards. It is a way of sharing the meal.

After my presentation, a classmate from Japan said that the tradition reminded her of a festival in her country called Obon, where families also remember their ancestors. I loved discovering that different cultures have similar ideas. For me, the altar is not about death. It is about not forgetting the people who made us who we are.

title: Is a Smartwatch Worth It? A Forum Discussion
paragraphs: Rosario_P: I'm thinking of buying a smartwatch for my birthday. The one I like costs 450 soles, which is a lot of money for me. I mainly want to count my steps and see notifications without taking out my phone. Is it really worth it, or am I just following a trend?

Marco_Runner: Definitely worth it for me. I've had mine for two years, and I use it every time I run. It shows my speed, my heart rate and the route, and I have improved my 5K time by four minutes. If you do any sport, you will use it a lot. Also, the battery lasts three days, which is longer than I expected.

Mei_L: I disagree. I bought one last year, and after the first month I stopped using it. The notifications were annoying because my wrist buzzed all the time, and I had to charge it every night. If you don't exercise, I think a simple sports watch or even your phone is enough. Also, some cheap models count steps badly.

Andean_Tom: I think both of you are right. A smartwatch is useful only if it solves a real problem for you. Before buying, write down what you want it for. If the list has only one or two things, it is probably cheaper to use an app. And please compare prices in different shops, because the same model can be fifty soles cheaper online.

Rosario_P: Thanks, everyone! I think I will wait a month and see whether I still want it. In the meantime, I'll try a free step-counting app and decide if I need more features. If I still want the watch after thirty days, I'll buy it. And if not, I'll save the money for a new pair of running shoes.

title: How I Ran My First Ten Kilometres
focus: Past simple, present perfect and modal deduction
paragraphs: Six months ago I couldn't run for ten minutes without stopping. This Sunday I finished my first ten-kilometre race in Medellín. I want to tell you how I did it, because if I can do it, you can do it too.

It started when my cousin Daniela challenged me to enter a race with her. I paid the entry fee, thirty thousand pesos, the same day, so I couldn't change my mind. We made a simple plan: to run three times a week, always in the morning, and to increase the distance a little every Sunday. At the beginning I could only run two kilometres.

The hardest moment came in the third month. My legs hurt, I was tired after school, and it rained for two weeks. One morning I stayed in bed and decided to quit. But Daniela called me and said, 'You have already run more than you ever imagined. Don't throw it away.' She was right, so I put on my shoes and went out in the rain.

On race day I woke up at four thirty because I was too nervous to sleep. There were thousands of people at the start, and the music was so loud that I couldn't hear my own thoughts. For the first five kilometres I felt great. After that, I wanted to stop. A man next to me, who must have been sixty, said, 'Slowly, but never stop.' I repeated those words in my head until I saw the finish line.

I finished in one hour and twelve minutes. It wasn't a fast time, but I cried when I crossed the line. Daniela finished ten minutes before me and was waiting with a banana and a big hug. My next goal is to improve my time by five minutes. If you have been thinking about starting, my advice is simple: choose a goal, find a partner, and take the first step this week.

title: A Letter to the Principal: Let's Start a Film Club
paragraphs: Dear Mrs Andrade,

I am writing to propose the creation of a film club at our school. I am a student in Year 11, and I have discussed the idea with more than thirty classmates, who have said that they would be interested in joining.

The club would meet every Friday from three to five o'clock in the school library. Each week, we would watch one film, and afterwards we would talk about it for twenty minutes. Every second week, we would choose a film in English with English subtitles, which would help students to improve their listening skills in a natural and enjoyable way.

We understand that the school has limited resources, so we have tried to keep the plan simple. The library already has a projector and a screen. We would only need permission to use the room and a teacher to supervise the sessions. In addition, we would collect a small amount of money, approximately forty dollars in total, for posters and snacks.

We would also respect copyright law and only show films that the school has the right to use. Mr Cevallos, our English teacher, has kindly said that he would be happy to help us choose suitable titles.

I believe that the club would not only be entertaining but also useful for the school community. It would offer a safe place for students to spend Friday afternoons, and it would encourage them to share their opinions respectfully. I would be grateful if you could consider our proposal and give us a short meeting to explain it in more detail.
Yours sincerely,
Kevin Morán

title: Summer Camp Counsellors Wanted
focus: Requirements and obligations: must, need to, have to
paragraphs: Camp Ondas, a summer camp near Florianópolis in southern Brazil, is looking for twelve counsellors for the summer season, from December to the end of February. If you love working with children and want to improve your English, this could be the perfect job for you.

What will you do? You will organise sports, art and nature activities for groups of ten children aged eight to twelve. You will also help children at mealtimes, and you will be responsible for their safety during beach trips. Every day starts at eight in the morning and finishes at five in the afternoon, with a two-hour break at lunchtime.

Who are we looking for? Candidates must be at least eighteen years old and must have some experience with children, for example as a volunteer or in a school club. You need an intermediate level of English, because about a third of our campers come from other countries. A first-aid certificate is useful but not necessary: we offer a free course in the first week.

What do we offer? We pay 1,800 reais per month, and we provide meals and a shared room near the camp. You will receive training before the campers arrive, and you will have one free day every week to enjoy the beach. At the end of the summer, we give each counsellor a letter of reference, which can help you in future job applications.

How to apply: send your CV and a short video, no longer than two minutes, in which you introduce yourself in English. Tell us why you would be a good counsellor and describe a time when you solved a problem with a group. The deadline is 15 November. We will invite the best candidates to an online interview during the following week.
Please note that we cannot accept applications without a video, and we will not answer phone calls. Good luck! We look forward to meeting you.

title: The Morning the Floor Moved
paragraphs: On Tuesday morning, Pilar was taking an English test in her classroom in Santiago when she noticed that the water in her bottle was moving. At first she thought she was imagining it. Then the windows began to shake, and the lights above her head moved from side to side.

'Under the tables!' shouted Mr Vargas, the teacher. Almost everybody knew exactly what to do because the school had practised the drill only a month before. Thirty students got down quickly, holding the legs of their tables with both hands. Pilar remembered the rule: protect your head and wait until the movement stops.

The tremor lasted about forty seconds, but it felt like ten minutes. Some students were crying, and Ignacio, who was sitting next to the door, couldn't move at all. He was standing in the middle of the room with his mouth open. Pilar crawled to him, took his hand and said, 'Come here, under my table. We're okay.'

When the movement stopped, Mr Vargas checked that nobody was injured. Then the class walked, without running, to the school yard, as the safety plan said. Teachers from other classrooms were already there, counting their students. In ten minutes, the principal confirmed that everyone was safe and that the building had no serious damage.

In the yard, Ignacio sat beside Pilar. 'I froze,' he said quietly. 'I practised the drill, but my body didn't listen.' Pilar smiled. 'It happens to many people. That's exactly why we practise. Next time, your body will remember.' That afternoon, the students didn't talk about the test. They talked about what they had learnt: that it is better to be prepared than to be surprised.

Later, Mr Vargas said that nobody had to finish the test that day. 'You have already passed a more important exam,' he said. Pilar kept thinking about his words on the bus home, and she decided to check that her family had an emergency bag ready.

title: The Night the Lighthouse Mattered
paragraphs: Amaru had never liked the sea until the summer he spent with his uncle Olegario, the last lighthouse keeper on that part of the southern coast of Chile. The lighthouse stood on a cliff, two hours by bus from the nearest town. There was no phone signal, and the only neighbours were seabirds.

His uncle had lived there for thirty years. Every evening he climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to check the lamp, and every morning he wrote the weather in a thick notebook. 'Machines can turn on a light,' he told Amaru, 'but they can't look at the sky and feel that a storm is coming.'

One night in February, Olegario woke Amaru at two o'clock. The wind was howling, and the waves were hitting the rocks with a noise like thunder. 'Put on your coat,' his uncle said. 'The radio says that a fishing boat has lost its engine.' They ran up the stairs, and Olegario turned the lamp to its strongest light.

For three hours they watched the dark water. Amaru's job was to hold the radio and tell his uncle everything that the captain said. The captain was afraid, but Olegario spoke to him in a calm, slow voice. 'Follow the light,' he repeated. 'The rocks are on your left. Stay on the right side of the beam.'

At five o'clock, a small boat with three tired fishermen appeared in the bay below the cliff. They had survived. Amaru jumped up and down and shouted until his throat hurt. Later, the captain climbed the steps and hugged them both. 'I have been a fisherman for forty years,' he said, 'and tonight I understood what a lighthouse really is.'

When summer ended, Amaru went home with a notebook of his own. On the first page he wrote the weather for the day, just as his uncle had taught him. He still loved the land, but now he also respected the sea.

title: Growing Up with Two Languages
paragraphs: Adriana Vega, eighteen, was born in Miami, but she speaks English with her friends, Spanish with her grandparents and a mix of both with her cousins. 'Spanglish is our own secret code,' she laughs. We asked her what it's like to grow up with two languages.

When she was little, Adriana sometimes felt confused. 'I used to mix words from both languages in the same sentence, and teachers corrected me,' she remembers. 'Now I know that it's normal for bilingual children. My brain is simply choosing the fastest word.'

Being bilingual has given her unusual responsibilities. Since she was twelve, she has translated at the doctor's, at the bank and at parent-teacher meetings for her grandparents. 'It was stressful at first, because I didn't know many medical words,' she says. 'But it taught me to listen carefully and to explain things clearly.'

She has also noticed some advantages. She can read menus, signs and songs in two languages, and she says that learning French at school has been easier than it was for her friends. 'Some studies suggest that bilingual people find it easier to learn a third language,' she says. 'I don't know if it's true for everybody, but it's true for me.'

However, she admits that it takes effort to keep both languages strong. 'When I stopped reading Spanish books at fourteen, my vocabulary started to disappear,' she explains. 'So now I read for twenty minutes a day in Spanish, even if I'm busy.' She is also learning to write short poems in Spanish. Her advice for families is simple: speak your home language proudly, because it is a gift that you can give to your children.

title: The Café Where Nothing Is Thrown Away
paragraphs: Leyla's headphones had stopped working after only eight months. The shop said that repairing them would cost more than buying new ones, so she was about to throw them away. Then her neighbour told her about a repair café in her district of Berlin, where volunteers fix broken things for free.

The café opens on the first Saturday of every month in a community centre. When Leyla arrived, the room was full of tables, tools and cups of tea. People of all ages were waiting with broken lamps, toasters, bicycles and even a violin. A sign on the wall said: 'Don't throw it away. Let's try to repair it together.'

A volunteer called Mr Weber, a retired engineer, looked at her headphones through a magnifying glass. 'The problem is a loose wire,' he said. But instead of repairing them himself, he gave Leyla a small soldering iron and showed her what to do. She was nervous because the iron was very hot, but after ten minutes she had fixed the wire.

'That's the idea of the café,' Mr Weber explained. 'We don't just repair objects. We teach people how to repair them. If you understand how something works, you will probably look after it better.' Leyla noticed that every volunteer was talking and laughing with the visitors. It felt more like a party than a workshop.

At the end, Leyla put two euros in the donation box, which pays for new tools and coffee. Her headphones were working perfectly, and she had learnt a new skill. On the way home, she thought about all the things in her house that were waiting in a drawer. 'Next month I'm bringing my brother's broken game controller,' she decided. 'And maybe I'll volunteer to help too.'
